moat.description: Global two-sided network in mobility and delivery with rider-driver liquidity that no rival can replicate at the same density — moat is real, autonomy is the existential question, and the Waymo relationship is the clearest crack since the June review.
moat.analysisSummary: Uber's moat is **network density across mobility and delivery in 70+ countries** — durable in the human-driven era, and still the default demand-aggregation layer into autonomy, though the partnership path is no longer one-sided:

analysisPoints.title: Liquidity Network Effects
analysisPoints.text: Uber's wait-times, surge dynamics, and supply density in major cities cannot be matched without simultaneous rider and driver acquisition at scale. Lyft, Bolt, and DiDi compete city-by-city; only Uber holds the global liquidity stack across both mobility and delivery.

analysisPoints.title: Cross-App Bundling and Membership
analysisPoints.text: Uber One bundles mobility + delivery + grocery + ad-supported value, creating cross-category retention. Uber One reached 50M members in Q1 2026 and now drives roughly half of total Mobility and Delivery gross bookings. The July 2026 Delivery Hero takeover offer (€41.50/share, ~$14.8B equity value, close targeted H2 2027) would nearly double dual mobility+delivery markets from 34 to 58 and extend the bundle into Korea, MENA, LatAm, and foodpanda Asia — pending regulatory clearance and the SSW carve-out of 14 overlapping markets.

analysisPoints.title: Autonomous Demand Layer — Partnership Thesis Under Stress
analysisPoints.text: Uber still positions itself as the consumer demand and dispatch layer for autonomy (Wayve, NVIDIA 100k-vehicle network targeting 2027, other AV partners). But the flagship Waymo relationship has frayed: the Phoenix pilot ended at its contracted term in May 2026 (confirmed late June), and a July 2026 FT report said Waymo has told Uber it intends to enter Austin and Atlanta on its own from January 2028 when the current exclusivity allows, with Uber expecting Waymo rides on its app through May 2028 agreement expiry. Tesla continues Cybercab production at Giga Texas and its own ride-hailing expansion in Austin, Dallas, and Houston, while Waymo delivers 500K+ paid robotaxi rides weekly on its own app. The demand-aggregator thesis is intact as a strategy; exclusivity with the leading US robotaxi operator is no longer the base case.

growth.description: Latest print remains Q1 2026 (reported May 2026); Q2 prints August 5. Gross bookings $53.7B, +25% YoY (+21% constant currency). Mobility +25% (+20% cc), Delivery +28% (+23% cc). Adj EBITDA $2.5B, +33% YoY, margin 4.6% of gross bookings. FCF a record $9.8B TTM; $3B buyback in Q1. Q2 guide was 18–22% constant-currency bookings growth and adj EBITDA $2.70–$2.80B. Post-print: Delivery Hero cash offer announced 16 July (99 combined markets, pro-forma 2025 gross bookings $236B, Non-GAAP EPS accretion targeted on close in H2 2027); Waymo partnership stress (Phoenix ended, Austin/Atlanta exclusivity set to lapse into own-app competition from 2028) is the new overhang into the print.

growthAnalysis.scoreDerivation: Base ~82 on a 17.5% midpoint of the 15–20% bookings CAGR — anchored to Q1's +21% constant-currency print and the guided 18–22% Q2 range, decayed for autonomy and Delivery Hero integration drag rather than extrapolated. +4 trajectory (all three drivers accelerating on the latest print) +4 margin (adj EBITDA +33%, 4.6% of bookings) −10 high autonomy risk (Waymo own-app path now dated to 2028 in Austin/Atlanta; Tesla Cybercab production continuing) = 80. The dual-TAM / Delivery Hero story is real but unpaid here — primaryType no longer scores, and the deal does not close until H2 2027.

growthAnalysis.keyRisk: Waymo has ended the Phoenix Uber pilot and, per a July 2026 FT report, has informed Uber it will enter Austin and Atlanta independently from January 2028; Tesla continues Cybercab volume production and its own consumer ride-hailing network in Texas metros. If Tesla scales direct-to-consumer demand aggregation or Waymo's own app displaces Uber on the densest US robotaxi routes, Uber loses pricing power on the highest-margin urban trips by 2028–29. Separately, the Delivery Hero offer (~$14.8B equity value, €14B bridge facility, close H2 2027) adds merger-control and leverage execution risk before any accretion lands.

valuation.description: At ~$70 Uber trades ~26% below the base case ($95) and ~33% below the ~$104 Wall Street average target (Strong Buy / Moderate Buy consensus), at ~21× consensus FY26 EPS (~$3.30) and ~7% FCF yield on record TTM FCF of ~$9.8B. The stock has been range-bound in the high-$60s to low-$70s since the June review — slid ~5% on the 24 July Waymo-walkaway report, supported on the 16 July Delivery Hero announcement — still ~31% below the $101.99 52-week high. Robotaxi fears remain the multiple compressor; Q1 fundamentals and the Delivery Hero optionality are not yet showing through in the price. Q2 prints 5 August.

peAnalysis.summary: Uber remains a free-cash compounder with network durability trading at a fear-discounted multiple. Since June the two new facts are Delivery Hero (optionality, H2 2027 close) and a clearer Waymo own-app path in Austin/Atlanta from 2028 — opposite forces on the same autonomy/platform question, neither yet visible in Q1's numbers.

learnedInterfaces.note: Consumer learning curve on rider app and habit formation is real but easily transferred.

businessLogic.note: Dispatch, surge, ETA prediction, and routing algorithms are differentiated but increasingly replicable by autonomy operators.

publicDataAccess.note: N/A — Uber is not a public-data access business.

talentScarcity.note: Marketplace engineering and operational scale talent is broadly available.

bundling.note: Uber One mobility + delivery + grocery + advertising bundle is genuinely differentiated; Delivery Hero would extend the dual-product footprint from 34 to 58 markets if the H2 2027 close lands — only DoorDash + Lyft attempt anything similar at much smaller scale today.

proprietaryData.note: Trip-level supply/demand data across 70+ countries is genuinely unique and feeds dispatch + pricing + autonomy partner integration.

regulatoryLockIn.note: Local rideshare licences, AV partnership integrations, and city-level relationships create switching friction in many markets.

networkEffects.note: Two-sided rider-driver liquidity in major cities is the textbook example of network effects; rivals struggle to replicate density without years of subsidy. Autonomy operators with their own apps (Waymo, Tesla) are the structural test of whether that liquidity still compounds on Uber's surface.

transactionEmbedding.note: Stored payment, defaults, and travel/expense corporate integrations make Uber the default rideshare for both consumers and enterprises.

systemOfRecord.note: Uber is the system of record for mobility identity and history for ~150M+ active monthly riders globally.

tenMoats.verdict: Uber's network, bundling, and transaction-embedding moats remain AI-resilient — language models do not erode rider-driver liquidity. The Delivery Hero offer would deepen the bundling moat geographically if it clears. The AI-era structural threat is still autonomy: robotaxis (Waymo, Tesla Cybercab) attack the human-driven mobility network that anchors the moat. Since June that threat has become more specific — Waymo's Phoenix pilot ended, and Austin/Atlanta exclusivity now has a dated end (own-app entry from January 2028). The thesis question is unchanged: whether Uber retains the consumer demand layer as autonomy commercialises. Diversified partners (Wayve, NVIDIA network) and trip-level data still support a durable aggregator role; Tesla vertical integration and Waymo's own-app expansion are the primary tail risks.
